title: From readiness to resilience: rethinking cybersecurity for the AI era
summary: Explore how DORA, NIS2 and emerging AI threats are reshaping cybersecurity requirements and why continuous resilience is critical for EU enterprises.
body_markdown:
One year ago, the European Union designated Kyndryl as one of 19 Critical Third-Party Providers under its[Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA)](https://www.eba.europa.eu/activities/direct-supervision-and-oversight/digital-operational-resilience-act) . DORA establishes comprehensive requirements for financial services entities and their critical services providers in areas of Information and Communications Technology (ICT) security, risk management, oversight and resilience. As a Critical Third-Party Provider, Kyndryl’s work includes supporting enterprise-wide governance, compliance and oversight activities for our banking and insurance customers in the EU.


Reflecting on the past year since this designation, the cybersecurity landscape has continued to evolve. Frontier AI models are[dramatically compressing the time](https://www.kyndryl.com/us/en/insights/articles/2026/05/frontier-ai-cybersecurity) available to identify and address vulnerabilities. At the same time, they offer defenders new tools to assess risk and build resilience.


Similar principles underpin the[EU’s NIS2 Directive](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/nis2-directive) , which “establishes a unified legal framework to uphold cybersecurity in 18 critical sectors across the EU \[and\] calls on Member States to define national cybersecurity strategies and collaborate with the EU for cross-border reaction and enforcement.” That’s a long way of saying that the EU’s core industries must take clearly defined steps to practice ongoing resilience to cyber attacks. This is what Kyndryl does for our customers every day.


[Kyndryl’s recent 2026-27 Readiness Report](https://www.kyndryl.com/us/en/insights/research/readiness-report) confirms that security concerns remain top of mind for the C-suite. But while three-quarters of senior leaders count on AI to help identify threats, more than half still worry their organizations can’t keep up. That probably helps explain why only about a quarter of leaders believe their organizations are fully prepared to defend against cyberattacks, representing an 11-point drop from last year.


Operational resilience is a continuous discipline rather than a one-time activity. As threats to IT and OT become more sophisticated, defending against them requires agility, foresight and preparation. Together, these capabilities define readiness and provide a blueprint for how Kyndryl operates.


Security is now integral to every part of the enterprise technology environment, from infrastructure and networks to suppliers, applications, data and AI. As AI operates on both sides of the cybersecurity equation, organizations need greater visibility into and control over their technology estates. Security tools must help enterprises correlate information and take corrective action quickly.

**Paul Savill**
Global Practice Leader for Cyber Resilience and Connectivity


### Building proactive resilience


As data moves across networks, through security controls and into applications, clouds and AI-infused platforms, it doesn’t recognize the traditional boundaries between network and security operations. Though not interchangeable, network performance problems and cybersecurity incidents can influence each other and disrupt business continuity.


To help our customers address this new reality of interconnected network and security challenges, Kyndryl opened a new[Cyber Defense Operations Center in Paris](https://www.kyndryl.com/us/en/about-us/news/2026/10/new-cyber-defense-operations-center-paris) . As the latest node in[Kyndryl’s global network of security operations centers](https://www.kyndryl.com/us/en/services/cyber-resilience/security-operations/center) , the Paris location provides organizations with convenient access to Kyndryl’s decades of experience in identifying and addressing anomalies across increasingly complex technology estates.


[Kyndryl Bridge](https://www.kyndryl.com/us/en/services/platform) supports the Paris center’s operations with vital cross-industry data from more than 1,400 enterprises, enabling the sophisticated pattern recognition required for optimal automation design and human decision-making. Customers also benefit from Kyndryl’s alliances with more than a dozen technology and solutions providers in disciplines such as threat detection, vulnerability management, security automation, incident response and network monitoring.


Finally, Kyndryl’s first operations center of its type in Europe helps address the data sovereignty requirements of regional customers. With the regulatory environment for AI and critical business operations in constant flux, the Paris center can provide customers with fit-for-purpose expertise and services that are flexible and globally scalable.


### Looking ahead


Findings from the Kyndryl 2026-27 Readiness Report, the stated mission of Kyndryl’s Cyber Defense Operations Centers and the latest regulations from the EU and elsewhere all underscore the need for cyber resilience by design.


The gaps between where many organizations stand and where they need to be are real. But closing them while building the flexibility that enables protective systems to adapt and scale is within reach. The first step is to recognize and clearly define the challenges ahead.
